newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian shares tumble to near pre-budget levels.
newsitem.headline: Indian shares tumble to near pre-budget levels.

text.p: Indian shares, which jumped 16 percent after last month's business-friendly budget, have lost much of those gains as foreign investors await key corporate earnings and an impending oil price rise, analysts said.
Bombay's benchmark stock index surged nearly 16 percent to an eight-month high of 4,029.56 in early March from a close of 3,474.79 on February 28, the day the budget was announced.

But the 30-share index has since tumbled around 350 points, or seven percent, and traders say foreign funds are maintaining a low profile. The index was trading 2.16 points lower at 3686.91 in late trade on Thursday.

"Just after the budget, a lot of people built speculative positions on the hope that foreign institutional investors (FIIs) would jump on the bandwagon," said Sridhar Narayan, investment analyst at mutual fund ITC Threadneedle.
"But the buying has not come through and it is not possible for speculators to maintain these positions."
In the federal budget for 1997/98 (April-March), Finance Minister P. Chidambaram slashed personal and corporate taxes beyond all market expectations.

Chidambaram withdrew a 7.5 percent corporate surcharge and removed a tax on dividend incomes. He raised the limits on FII investments in Indian firms to 30 percent from 24 percent and allowed companies to buy back their own shares.
"Speculators built up huge positions expecting FIIs to come in droves," said the head of sales at a foreign brokerage.
Foreign funds initially flowed in, making net purchases of $101.1 million from March 1-12 against $88.8 million in the entire month of February.
But they chose to hold back as the rally gathered steam.
"Foreign funds are expecting the market to fall when the petrol price hike is announced and see that as an opportunity to enter at a lower level," said ITC Threadneedle's Narayan.

The budget sidestepped the worrying issue of the burgeoning oil pool deficit, estimated to exceed 155 billion ($4.3 billion) rupees by March 31. The oil pool deficit is effectively the amount in subsidies the government owes oil companies for selling products below world prices.
Oil analysts say a product price rise is inevitable.
"Everybody is almost sure that the oil price hike is going to happen soon" said one analyst. "Earnings announcements are also going to be dismal and savvy investors are just waiting it out."
High interest rates, an industrial slowdown and lower global commodity prices have hit the profits of leading companies in the financial year beginning April 1, 1996.
Key results for 1996/97 are expected in April and May.
Analysts said some investors were focused on the long-awaited issue of global depositary receipts (GDRs) from state-run overseas telecommunications monopoly Videsh Sanchar Nigam Ltd.
The GDR issue, which is likely to raise around $550 million, is due to be priced on March 24. Investment bankers say it has already been oversubscribed about 2.5 times.
"A lot of money is going into VSNL," said Sandeep Nanda, head of research at Natwest Markets.
